messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar was a 34-year-old Middle Eastern publisher, married and living in a busy American city, who came to treatment nearly a year after the night his younger brother was assaulted outside an apartment building on the way home from work. Omar had been waiting for him by the window when the call came from the hospital: his brother had been found half-conscious in the stairwell, stripped of his wallet and phone, with bruising that made it look as though he had fought back. Omar never saw the attack itself, but what happened after the call lodged in him with a force that made the event feel incomplete and impossible to organize. When he tried to remember, the scene came back in disconnected pieces — the fluorescent lights in the emergency bay, his brother’s torn shirt, the smell of antiseptic, a police officer saying “possible blade,” his own hands shaking around a paper cup — and those fragments would not settle into a single account. Sometimes the memory arrived as though it were playing in front of him like a film on a loop, each replay ending at the same point of helplessness. At other times, especially when he became overtired at the end of a long workday, he would hear the sounds from that night in his head, as if the words and tones had been pressed into his mind and could still be replayed without warning.

In the months that followed, Omar noticed that the memory did not stay in the past. It pulled his attention toward anything that might signal danger, and his mind began scanning the world the way he had scanned the hospital corridor for news. He studied people’s faces and body language in a way that felt urgent and exhausting, trying to decide at a glance who might be a threat, who was angry, who might suddenly move closer. He noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, his eyes catching on knives in restaurant windows, broken glass near the curb, a metal rod on a subway platform. The more vivid the memory became, the more certain he was that danger could appear without warning, and that certainty made it harder for him to tolerate places where he could not quickly assess the risk. He avoided going anywhere unfamiliar, turning down invitations, refusing new delivery routes for work, and insisting on restaurants and shops he already knew because unknown spaces felt unreadable and therefore unsafe. The caution did not feel irrational to him; it felt like the only reason he had not missed something important before.

Those habits sharpened when his triggers were present. Being naked, especially while dressing or stepping out of the shower, left him feeling exposed in a way that echoed the vulnerability he associated with his brother’s injury, and his mind immediately went back to the night he could not protect him. Riding the bus produced the same tightening in his chest, because he could not control who boarded, who sat behind him, or what someone might be concealing; on crowded rides to work he would scan every face and every bag, then shift his attention to the exits and any object that could be used as a weapon. When he was very tired, his guard felt thin and the memory fragments came faster, which only made him more watchful. After a replayed memory or one of those intrusive sounds, he became even more alert to threat, as if the return of the scene proved that danger was still near. That heightened vigilance made the triggers more powerful, because once he had spent an hour searching faces on the bus or checking unfamiliar doorways on his way to a client meeting, he was more likely to notice the next sign of vulnerability or threat and feel the old dread rush back.

Work and home life had both narrowed around these loops. As a publisher, Omar used to move easily between offices, author events, and unfamiliar neighborhoods, but now he planned every route and avoided assignments that would take him to places he had not already mentally mapped. He left the office earlier than he wanted so he would not be too tired for the bus ride home, and by evening he was often drained from the effort of watching the world so closely. His wife noticed that he had become quieter and less spontaneous, more preoccupied with checking locks and glancing toward windows when he heard footsteps in the hall. Omar had come to fear that if he let his attention slip, he would miss the one sign that mattered, and that fear kept his mind locked on scanning, replaying, and bracing. By the time he sought help, he was sleeping poorly, avoiding ordinary routines that made him feel exposed, and feeling increasingly trapped by the sense that the world could turn dangerous in an instant. What finally brought him in was the realization that he was no longer just afraid for his brother; he was afraid that his life had become organized around the same helplessness, and he wanted to stop living as though every face, every bus ride, and every unfamiliar street were the beginning of another disaster.
